name: Nihonium

discovery.discoverer: Kosuke Morita and team, RIKEN, Japan

occurrence: Does not occur naturally; produced only via particle accelerator fusion, atom by atom.
majorUses: No practical applications — pure superheavy-element research
safetyNotes: Intensely radioactive; observed only as individual atoms with sub-second half-lives.
notableCharacteristics: Named after Japan itself ('Nihon' is Japanese for Japan) — the first element named by and for an Asian country's research team.
ncertRelevance: first element named after an Asian country
whyHere: Predicted to sit in Group 13 below thallium, nihonium is expected to show a similarly variable preference between +1 and +3 oxidation states, following the trend of increasingly stable lower oxidation states down heavy p-block groups.
didYouKnow: RIKEN's discovery of nihonium in 2004 (confirmed in 2015) made Japan the first Asian country to have the naming rights for a new chemical element, a point of considerable national scientific pride.
genZNote: First element ever named by and for an Asian country. Japan earned this one after years of painstaking accelerator work.
